Aerial Wildlife Survey Report
Wildlife Management Unit 158 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2024)
Classification: Public
Background
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 158 (Three Hills) spans an 
area of 1,777 km2 in south-central AB roughly between the 
Town of Trochu and City of Drumheller. The WMU includes 
land south of highway 585, east of highway 21, and west of 
highway 56. The southern boundary follows highway 9 south 
of Drumheller. The Red Deer River, with associated coulee 
systems, runs in a southeasterly direction roughly bisecting 
the WMU. Ghostpine, Threehills, Kneehills, and Michichi 
creeks, all with associated coulee systems, pass through 
the WMU joining the mainstem Red Deer River. The WMU is 
within the northern fescue subregion of the grasslands natural 
region and contains large expanses of cultivated cropland. 
Native habitats and badland formations occur in the river 
valley, creek valleys, and associated coulee systems. The 
Tolman Badlands Heritage Rangeland Natural Area occurs 
along the mainstem Red Deer River and Midland Provincial 
Park is located adjacent to the City of Drumheller. Chronic 
Wasting Disease (CWD) was first detected within WMU 158 
in 2015 (one positive) and has been increasing in prevalence 
since that time with 32 CWD positive deer in 2020. The 
established population goals for WMU 158 are pre-hunting 
season populations of 1,700 mule deer, 400 white-tailed deer, 
and 50 moose.
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, and 
moose) was last conducted for WMU 158 in December 2015. 
The objective of the February 2024 survey was to assess the 
status of ungulate populations in WMU 158 by determining 
estimates for abundance, density, and age-sex composition. 
We also recorded observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including carnivores, 
game birds, and sensitive or at-risk species.
Survey Method
A rotary wing transect survey was conducted February 12-13, 
2024, flying 32 east-west lines at 1.6 km intervals with an 
800 m wide survey strip. This resulted in 48% coverage of 
the unit, and a total survey effort of 1,065 linear km. At each 
observation point, ungulates were classified by species, and 
when possible, sex and age was recorded. Antler size for 
deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or 
both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more points; antlers 
inside ears) or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of 
ears). Because transects varied in length, the average density 
(R; #/km2) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose was 
calculated by summing the total animals counted per transect 
(∑x) by total area searched (length of transects multiplied by 
800 m survey strip [∑z]) (see Jolly 1969). For a population 
estimate (unequal sized units, sampling without replacement), 
the average density (R) was multiplied by the overall area of 
the WMU (Z). The width of the 90% confidence interval was 
calculated by multiplying the t statistic for the left-tailed inverse 
of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; 
without replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq 
root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-
2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number of possible transects given 
100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.
Results
Mule Deer
A total of 592 mule deer (222 does, 112 fawns, 99 bucks, 159 
unclassified) were observed in 60 groups (range 1-33). The 
estimated density was 0.70 mule deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 1,235 individuals (90% CI 961 – 1,510), 
representing a 47% decrease from the population estimate 
in 2016. A total of 433 mule deer were successfully classified 
and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 45:100:50. 
That results in an estimated 2023/2024 early winter mule 
deer population of 283 bucks, 634 does, and 319 fawns. Of 
the 99 mule deer bucks classified, 32 (32%) were classified 
‘small’, 51 (52%) ‘medium’, and 16 (16%) ‘large’. These results 
indicate the WMU 158 mule deer population has experienced 
a significant decline since 2015 and is currently below the 
established management goal. Further, there has been a 
substantial decline in the buck:doe ratio from 73:100 in 2015 
to 45:100 in 2024, although that difference is likely in part due 
to the late timing of the 2024 survey, with some bucks having 
shed antlers and being indistinguishable from does. Not only 
has the observed abundance of mule deer bucks decreased 
substantially from 341 in December 2015 to 99 in 2024, but 
the age structure of bucks has also changed towards younger 
cohorts. In the 2015 survey, 37% of classified bucks were 
“medium” antler size and 28% were “large”, compared to 51% 
“medium” and 16% “large” in 2024. That difference in antler 
classification is likely due in part to the lateness of the 2024 
survey (February 12-13) and fact that older bucks tend to shed 
antlers earlier than younger bucks. However, the shift in age 
structure also could be due to increasing prevalence of CWD 
in the unit and increased hunter harvest of bucks since 2015.

White-tailed Deer
A total of 129 white-tailed deer (55 does, 28 fawns, 20 bucks, 
26 unclassified) were observed in 19 groups (range 1-25). 
The estimated density was 0.15 deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 269 individuals (90% CI 175 – 364), 
representing a 40% decrease from the population estimate 
in 2016. A total of 103 white-tailed deer were successfully 
classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 
36:100:51. That results in an estimated 2023/2024 early winter 
white-tailed deer population of 52 bucks, 143 does, and 73 
fawns. Of the 20 white-tailed deer bucks classified, 8 (40%) 
were classified ‘small’ and 12 (60%) were ‘medium’. These 
results indicate the WMU 158 white-tailed deer population has 
experienced a significant decline since 2015 and is currently 
below the established management goal.
Moose
A total of 24 moose were observed in 15 groups (range 1-3). 
The estimated density was 0.03 moose/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 51 individuals (90% CI 34 – 66). Twenty 
moose were successfully classified and the bull:cow:calf ratio 
was estimated to be 50:100:100. That results in an estimated 
2023/2024 early winter moose population of 8 bulls, 16 cows, 
and 16 calves. When interpreting the data, consideration 
should be given to the low sample of moose observed and 
how it may impact population, density, and sex ratio estimates. 
The survey results demonstrate there is a relatively low 
abundance of moose in the WMU. However, the estimate in 
2024 is very similar to the survey conducted in 2015 indicating 
a stable moose population.
Other species observations that occurred within the survey 
area include 22 sharp-tailed grouse, 26 coyote, and one bald 
eagle. No elk or pronghorn were observed during this survey.
